echoes.note: 2:6 'who will pay back to everyone according to their works' is a near-verbatim citation of Ps 62:12 (LXX 61:13), 'for you repay to each according to his work' — the foundational judgment maxim Paul deploys against the presumptuous judge.

2:6 equally cites Prov 24:12, 'will he not repay each according to his deeds?' — joint source with Ps 62:12; Prov adds the 'God who weighs the heart / does he not know?' frame that suits Paul's argument about secret motives (cf. 2:16).

2:11 'there is no partiality with God' echoes Deut 10:17, 'God of gods... who shows no partiality (ou thaumazei prosopon) and takes no bribe' — the classic OT divine-impartiality formula underwriting Jew-and-Greek equality before judgment.

2:11 also reflects Jehoshaphat's charge, 'with the LORD our God there is no injustice or partiality (prosopolempsia) or taking of bribes' — a near-technical Greek precedent for Paul's coined prosopolempsia.

2:4 'riches of his goodness, forbearance, and patience' draws on the covenant self-revelation 'a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger (makrothymos), abounding in steadfast love' — the divine attribute of forbearance Paul says should lead to repentance, not presumption.

2:4 'goodness... forbearance... leads to repentance' closely tracks Wisdom of Solomon 11:23, 'you overlook the sins of men so that they may repent,' and 12:10's gift of 'space for repentance' — Second Temple theology of divine patience Paul reuses and then turns critically against Israel.

2:5 'treasuring up for yourself wrath in the day of wrath' echoes the Song of Moses, 'Is not this laid up in store with me, sealed up in my treasuries? Vengeance is mine,' the image of stored-up requital for a day of reckoning (Paul quotes the same verse at 12:19).

2:5 'day of wrath, revelation, and of the righteous judgment of God' draws on the Day-of-the-LORD oracle, 'that day is a day of wrath... of distress and anguish,' whose vocabulary (wrath, distress/anguish, cf. 2:9) saturates Paul's judgment scene.

2:5 'your hardness and unrepentant heart' may evoke the recurrent indictment of Israel's stubbornness (sklerokardia / hard neck), e.g. Deut 9:6,13,27; an echo Paul ironically applies to the self-confident judge.

2:6 repayment 'according to works' is reinforced by Jer 17:10, 'I the LORD search the heart... to give to each according to his ways, according to the fruit of his deeds' — joining heart-searching to works-recompense, both themes operative in Rom 2.

2:6 'according to their works' resonates with Jer 32:19 (LXX 39:19), 'whose eyes are open to all the ways of men, to reward every man according to his ways and the fruit of his deeds' — another witness to the judgment-by-works topos.

2:6 recompense by works also appears in Elihu's speech, 'for according to the work of a man he will repay him,' immediately followed (34:19) by God showing no partiality to princes — a striking pairing of Paul's two themes (works + impartiality).

2:6 'according to works' is closely paralleled by Sirach 16:12-14, 'he judges a man according to his deeds... he makes room for every act of mercy; everyone receives according to his deeds' — Second Temple crystallization of the same recompense doctrine.

2:11 'no partiality' is anticipated by Sirach 35:12-13 (LXX 35:15-16), 'the Lord is the judge, and with him is no partiality; he will not show partiality to the poor' — Second Temple restatement of the impartiality formula in a judgment context.

2:13 'the doers of the law will be justified' echoes the Torah principle 'the person who does them shall live by them' — the do-and-live logic (which Paul cites directly at 10:5; Gal 3:12) standing behind 'doers' over 'hearers.'

2:13 hearing-versus-doing reflects Moses' charge to 'listen (hear) to the statutes... and do them, that you may live,' the Deuteronomic pairing of shema and asah that Paul splits to indict mere hearers.

2:14-15 Gentiles 'a law to themselves' with the law's work 'in their hearts' faintly recalls Deut 30:11-14, 'the word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it' — the nearness/internality of the commandment (Paul quotes this at 10:6-8), here generalized to conscience.

2:15 'the work of the law written in their hearts' verbally echoes the new-covenant promise 'I will put my law within them, and on their hearts I will write it' — though Paul applies the imagery to Gentiles' moral intuition rather than Israel's eschatological renewal, the borrowing is deliberate and ironic.

2:16 'God will judge the secrets of men' draws on Qoheleth's conclusion, 'God will bring every deed into judgment, with every secret thing, whether good or evil' — secret-deed judgment as the climax of the wisdom tradition.
2:16 judging 'the secrets of men' echoes Ps 44:21 (LXX 43:22), 'would not God discover this? For he knows the secrets of the heart' — divine knowledge of hidden things grounding the verdict.

2:16 'judge the secrets' parallels Wisdom of Solomon 1:6-9, 'God is witness of his inmost feelings... a hearing reaches the Lord... and the report of his words comes to the Lord to convict him of his lawless deeds' — Second Temple scrutiny of inner thoughts at judgment.

2:16 God judging hidden 'secrets' resonates with 'man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart' — the principle of inward divine sight underlying Paul's contrast between outward and inward (developed at 2:28-29).

2:16 secret-judgment overlaps with Jer 17:10, 'I the LORD search the heart and test the mind' — heart-searching paired with works-recompense, already noted at 2:6 and reinforcing the pericope's frame.

2:24 'the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you, just as it is written' is an explicit formula-citation of Isa 52:5 LXX, 'because of you my name is continually blasphemed among the nations' — Paul's clinching scriptural proof of the indictment.

2:24 the profaning of God's name among the nations is reinforced by Ezek 36:20-23, 'they profaned my holy name... wherever they came among the nations' — the same prophetic logic (Israel's conduct dishonoring God before the Gentiles), and Ezek 36's heart/spirit renewal also feeds 2:29.

2:21-22 'you who teach another, don't you teach yourself? You who preach don't steal, do you steal?... commit adultery?' closely mirrors Ps 50:16-21 (LXX 49), 'what right have you to recite my statutes...? you keep company with thieves... and with adulterers' — God's rebuke of the hypocrite who recites the law while breaking it.

2:19 'a guide of the blind, a light to those in darkness' draws on the Servant's vocation 'a light to the nations, to open the eyes that are blind, to bring out... those who sit in darkness' — Israel's self-understanding as light to the Gentiles, which Paul ironizes.

2:19 'a light to those in darkness' also echoes Isa 49:6, 'I will make you a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth' — the Servant-Israel light-to-Gentiles motif Paul invokes only to expose the teacher's failure.

2:19 the irony deepens with Isa 42:19, 'who is blind but my servant... who is blind as the dedicated one?' — the would-be guide of the blind is himself the blind servant; a faint counter-echo within the same Isaianic context.

2:22 'you who abhor idols, do you rob temples?' reflects Deut 7:25-26, 'the carved images of their gods you shall burn... you shall utterly abhor it (bdelysse), for it is an abomination' — the very verb of abhorring idols (bdelyssomenos) Paul uses, sharpening the charge of temple-robbing inconsistency.

2:29 'circumcision is that of the heart' directly echoes Moses' command 'circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no longer stubborn' — the foundational text spiritualizing circumcision (note the proximity to Deut 10:17's impartiality, used at 2:11).

2:29 heart-circumcision in the Spirit draws on Deut 30:6, 'the LORD your God will circumcise your heart... so that you will love the LORD' — the promised divine (eschatological, Spirit-effected) circumcision, matching Paul's 'in the spirit not the letter.'

2:29 'circumcision of the heart' echoes Jer 4:4, 'circumcise yourselves to the LORD; remove the foreskin of your hearts' — prophetic demand for inward circumcision lest wrath go forth, fitting Paul's wrath-and-heart argument.

2:25-29 the worthlessness of fleshly circumcision without obedience reflects Jer 9:25-26, 'I will punish all who are circumcised merely in the flesh... for all these nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart' — exactly Paul's leveling of circumcised and uncircumcised by the heart criterion.

2:29 inward circumcision recalls Lev 26:41, 'if then their uncircumcised heart is humbled and they make amends for their iniquity' — the Holiness Code's notion of an uncircumcised heart needing humbling, a Torah basis for the heart/flesh distinction.

2:25-29 the pairing 'uncircumcised in heart and flesh' appears in Ezek 44:7-9 barring those 'uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh' from the sanctuary — the dual (heart/flesh) circumcision distinction Paul exploits.

2:29 'in the spirit, not in the letter' echoes the new-heart promise, 'I will give you a new heart... and put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes' — Spirit-wrought interior obedience over external observance.

2:25-29 the whole argument presupposes and reinterprets the Abrahamic covenant of circumcision in the flesh (Gen 17, 'every male shall be circumcised... in your flesh an everlasting covenant') — Paul figurally relocates the 'everlasting covenant' sign from flesh to heart/Spirit.

2:29 'whose praise is not from men but from God' likely plays on the etymology of 'Jew' (Judah/Yehudah), named in Gen 29:35 when Leah says 'this time I will praise the LORD' — the true Jew is the one of genuine praise, a Hebrew wordplay (Judah = praise; cf. Gen 49:8).
